flagged.evidence: The item calls the countable-partition definition “genuinely stronger,” but the two suprema always agree. For any countable partition E=⨆E_n, the finite partition E_0,...,E_N,⋃_{n>N}E_n has sum at least Σ_{n=0}^N|ν(E_n)|. Letting N tend to infinity shows the finite-partition supremum is at least that countable partition's sum; the reverse inequality is immediate because finite partitions are countable. Steps 1.1–2.1 establish only nonattainment by finite partitions, not a larger countable-partition supremum.

The definition applies to arbitrary signed measures and writes Σ|ν(E_n)|. The cited signed-measure definition permits ν(E)=+∞, while def-extended-reals states that there is “no ... absolute value on overline R” and that undefined cases need an explicit hypothesis. Thus for the counting measure on N, regarded as a signed measure, the one-piece partition {N} requires |+∞|, which this library has not defined.

It defines ∫s dν=Σc_jν(E_j) for every complex simple s and every signed measure. For X=N with counting measure ν and s=i·1_X, its canonical representation requires i·ν(X)=i·(+∞). def-extended-reals defines only partial real extended arithmetic and says “Nothing else is defined”; no complex multiple of an infinite signed-measure value is defined. Even a zero level set can require the explicitly undefined product 0·(+∞).

The step says that {1} and {-1} “gives a Hahn decomposition” on R. But the cited Hahn theorem requires P∩N=∅ and P∪N=X. Here {1}∪{-1}≠R; the remaining zero-measure set must be assigned to one of the two Hahn pieces. The displayed pair is therefore not a Hahn decomposition as claimed.

The proof defines I_q using membership of (-i)^qz_n in the closed first quadrant and then says the A_q form a finite partition. Boundary values belong to more than one such closed quadrant: if z_n=1, then n∈I_0 and n∈I_3 because 1 and i are both in the closed first quadrant. Hence A_0 and A_3 overlap. The later estimate can be retained with an overlapping cover or disjoint quadrant convention, so this is a nonfatal proof-step error.
